title: Start here
summary: Three repositories, one data contract and the order in which to set them up.
text: Start here How to set up a decompilation repository that builds in a private environment, accepts reviewed contributions and publishes its progress to this site. This guide is written for someone, or some agent, dropped into an empty repository with a game binary and no other context. Followed in order, it ends with a repository whose every push to main builds the target, verifies it byte for byte, measures it with objdiff and publishes the measurement to the progress site. The only things it cannot decide for you are your project's parameters: the platform, the compiler versions and tooling, the split configuration, the target ids and the presentation. Everything else is specified exactly, and every command, file name, field and secret named here matches the shipped code. The three repositories Each game is three repositories. Two are yours; the third is shared by every game on the site. Repository Visibility Holds owner/game public Source, headers, target configuration, tools and CI. The only place contributors work. owner/game-build private The original executables and the toolchain, built into a container image on GitHub Container Registry. Also private. mitsevox/decomp-data public, shared The published measurements of every game, served by GitHub Pages at https://mitsevox.github.io/decomp-data/ . The site itself, mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io , is a static page that reads the data repository at view time. It also hosts the publish action and the data contract that the producer uses. Adding a game changes nothing in the site repository. owner/game (public) owner/game-build (private) push to main push to main validate.yml image.yml plan: which targets changed docker build: /orig/<target>/..., toolchain tests: tool tests push ghcr.io/owner/game-build:main, print digest Validate <target>, inside the image <--- referenced by digest copy and verify the original configure, build, check the executable hash objdiff report -> build/<target>/report.json publish action (main only) -----------> mitsevox/decomp-data (public) data/game/<target>/latest.json, history.json, map.json data/game/game.json, index.json deploy.yml -> GitHub Pages ^ mitsevox.github.io/games/game/ reads /decomp-data/ at view time Placeholders used throughout Placeholder Stands for owner/game your public source repository owner/game-build your private build-image repository OWNER_LOGIN the owner's GitHub login game the game's slug on the site, [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]* GAME01-rev0 a target id, [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ ; GAME01 is its label, 0 its revision ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:... the build image, always referenced by digest DATA_APP_CLIENT_ID , DATA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY the repository variable and secret that hold the publishing credential (names are yours to choose) The examples are for a GameCube target built with decomp-toolkit and dtk-template, because that is what the reference repositories use. Another platform changes the toolchain, the original's path inside the image and the build commands; it changes nothing in CI structure, publishing or the site. The setup path Repository layout : create the public repository with the tracked and ignored paths. Targets : write config/targets.json , config/site.json and config/ci-targets.json . Build environment : create the private repository, build the image, make the package readable by the public repository, note the digest. Build, verify, measure : get a byte-identical relink locally and an objdiff report.json . Evidence and the contribution workflow : adopt AGENTS.md , CONTRIBUTING.md and the PR template. Review gate : install review.yml , set REVIEW_OWNER , make the status required. CI : install validate.yml with your image digest and build commands. Publishing : create the GitHub App credential, add the variable and secret, push to main . The site : check the page, commit cover art to the data repository. Data contract describes what the publish action writes; Troubleshooting lists the failure messages; Starter kit is the download with every copyable file. What done looks like A push to main runs Validate with the jobs Plan affected targets , Tool tests , Validate <target id> for each affected active target and Validate targets . The Validate <target id> job ends with Publish to the site , and the data repository gains a commit titled game GAME01-rev0: <sha>, <n>% code linked . The data repository's Deploy workflow runs, and https://mitsevox.github.io/games/game/ shows the new measurement within a few minutes. A pull request runs the same build without the publish step, and cannot merge until Validate targets and Owner review clearance pass. Glossary Term Meaning target One original binary the project matches: a game id plus a disc revision, region or platform. Identified by a stable id. active A target that is built, verified and measured. planned and archived targets are listed on the page but never built. original The unmodified executable, kept in the private image and never in the public repository. build image The private container image with the originals and the toolchain, referenced by digest. objdiff report report.json , written by objdiff-cli report generate ; the only measurement input the publish action reads. linked Bytes of units that compile from source into the byte-identical executable ( Matching objects). matched Bytes that match exactly whether linked or not (exact functions in NonMatching units count). fuzzy Size-weighted similarity of every function and data section. publish action mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/publish , which converts the report into the contract files and pushes them. data repository mitsevox/decomp-data : one directory per game and target, served by Pages. contract The schema-1 file format ( contract/README.md ); publish.py check is its executable form. review record A PR comment that starts with Revision: and an Accuracy: or Hostile: verdict. owner clearance The owner's comment that names the head revision and two passing review records. REVIEW_OWNER The login whose clearance comments the review gate trusts. merge gate Optional: an agent acting under the owner's account to which the owner delegates clearance and merging. Using this guide with an agent Give the agent the whole guide as one Markdown file , the starter archive and the project parameters. The starter kit has a prompt. An agent cannot obtain the original, create the private repository, install the GitHub App or set repository settings on its own; the guide marks those steps as the owner's.

title: Repository layout
summary: What the public repository tracks, what it ignores and where each file lives.
text: Repository layout What the public repository tracks, what it ignores and where each file lives. The public repository This is the layout of a GameCube or Wii project built with dtk-template , with the files this guide adds marked. Keep the names: the CI workflow, the tools and the publish action refer to them. game/ README.md target, owner, build commands CONTRIBUTING.md contribution, review and merge policy (starter) AGENTS.md agent instructions (starter) .gitignore originals, generated output (starter) .gitattributes optional: line endings for toolkit files configure.py build configuration: libraries, objects, flags (dtk-template) config/ targets.json the target list, schema 1 (starter) site.json presentation on the site (starter) ci-targets.json which paths affect which target (starter) README.md evidence record format (starter) GAME01-rev0/ one directory per target, named by its id config.yml decomp-toolkit project: original path, hash, symbols, splits splits.txt, symbols.txt toolkit inputs build.sha1 expected hash of the built executable evidence.tsv curated claims src/ reconstructed source, complete and partial include/ shared declarations tools/ __init__.py (starter) targets.py reads and validates config/targets.json (starter) ci_targets.py selects affected targets in CI (starter) verify_target.py checks the original's SHA-1 (starter) measuring_tools.py lists tool versions for provenance (starter) project.py, ninja_syntax.py, download_tool.py, ... dtk-template tests/ test_targets.py (starter) review_gate.mjs (starter) docs/ durable documentation orig/GAME01-rev0/.gitkeep where the original goes locally; the file itself is ignored build/ generated, ignored .github/ workflows/validate.yml (starter) workflows/review.yml (starter) pull_request_template.md (starter) Three directories are keyed by the target id and nothing else: config/<target id>/ for inputs, orig/<target id>/ for the original, build/<target id>/ for everything generated, including build.ninja , objdiff.json and report.json . Switching targets never overwrites another target's files. This holds for a project with a single target too: there is no flat, unkeyed layout to grow out of later. Tracked and ignored Public Git holds reviewed source, headers, tools, curated evidence and configuration. It never holds: original executables, disc images or extracted assets ( orig/*/* is ignored; orig/<target id>/.gitkeep marks the directory); generated objects, build directories, objdiff and editor configuration ( build/ , build.ninja , objdiff.json , compile_commands.json ); complete debug exports, private analysis databases or discarded trial variants. The starter .gitignore covers these for a dtk-template project. A .gitignore entry does not remove a file already tracked; inspect git status before every commit that touches orig/ . The private repository game-build/ Dockerfile originals + toolchain into one image (starter) .github/workflows/image.yml builds, verifies and publishes the image (starter) README.md (starter) orig/GAME01-rev0/main.dol the original, committed here The private repository is the only place the original is stored. It is committed there because the image build copies it in and checks its hash; see Build environment . The data repository You do not create this one; the publish action writes into it. For reference, it looks like this after the first publish of game : decomp-data/ index.json {"schema": 1, "games": ["game", ...]} .nojekyll .github/workflows/deploy.yml Pages deploy on every push data/game/game.json presentation and the target list data/game/cover.webp optional, committed by hand data/game/GAME01-rev0/latest.json data/game/GAME01-rev0/history.json data/game/GAME01-rev0/map.json Only active targets have a directory. See Data contract . Naming Target ids are [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ and stable forever: they name directories, the site's ?target= value and the data directory. <label>-rev<revision> is the convention the examples use. The slug is [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]* and names the game on the site: /games/<slug>/ and data/<slug>/ . Unknown functions keep tool-generated address labels ( fn_<hex> with decomp-toolkit, func_<hex> with splat). The publish action counts a function as named only when its symbol is not such a label, so a descriptive name is a claim and needs evidence. Files under src/ use recovered paths when established; a descriptive file name counts as named while its boundaries remain provisional.

title: Targets
summary: config/targets.json, config/site.json and config/ci-targets.json, field by field.
text: Targets config/targets.json , config/site.json and config/ci-targets.json , field by field. A target is one original binary. A game with one disc revision has one target; a second revision, region or platform is a second entry, never a replacement. Lay out every project as multi-target from the first commit, even with one disc. The target id always carries its revision ( GAME01-rev0 , never a bare GAME01 ), every per-target path is keyed by that id, and targets.json is a list with one entry. Adding a revision or region later is then a new folder and a new list entry; nothing is renamed or moved. A target id is permanent once published, because it names the target's directory in the data repository and the ?target= value in its URLs. The three files below are the producer's only inputs to the site apart from the objdiff report. Copies with placeholders are in the starter kit . config/targets.json { "schema": 1, "defaultTarget": "GAME01-rev0", "targets": [ {"id": "GAME01-rev0", "platform": "gamecube", "label": "GAME01", "region": "USA", "revision": "0", "sha1": "0000000000000000000000000000000000000000", "status": "active"}, {"id": "GAME01-rev1", "platform": "gamecube", "label": "GAME01", "region": "USA", "revision": "1", "sha1": "1111111111111111111111111111111111111111", "status": "planned"} ] } Field Meaning Rule schema Format version Always 1 defaultTarget The target the game page and hub card show first Must be listed, and must be active id The target's identity: directory names, ?target= , the data directory [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ , unique, never changed once published platform Lower-case platform name [a-z0-9]+ , for example gamecube , wii , ps2 label Display: the game id on disc; the target picker groups by it Non-empty string region Display Non-empty string revision Display: the disc revision, unrelated to Git revisions; the picker groups by it under label Non-empty string sha1 SHA-1 of the original executable 40 lower-case hex digits status active : built, verified, measured, published. planned or archived : listed on the page, never built One of the three Two readers validate this file and both must accept it. tools/targets.py (starter) rejects any other field, requires exactly schema , defaultTarget and targets at the top level, and requires defaultTarget to be active. The publish action's publish.py reads the seven fields above, requires the default to be listed and writes the list verbatim into game.json . Run python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py' after every edit: tests/test_targets.py loads the file. Every active target needs a directory config/<id>/ , an original in the build image at /orig/<id>/<original path> , and an entry in config/ci-targets.json . A planned or archived target needs only the ci-targets.json entry (the planner requires every listed target to be covered) and may have an empty config/<id>/ . To find the SHA-1 of an original: sha1sum /path/to/main.dol # Linux shasum -a 1 /path/to/main.dol # macOS config/site.json { "schema": 1, "slug": "game", "title": "A Game: Full Title", "shortTitle": "A Game", "console": "GameCube", "year": "2002", "contributions": {"accepting": false}, "artwork": {"cover": "cover.webp", "width": 1112, "height": 1600} } Field Meaning Rule schema Format version 1 slug The game's name everywhere on the site and in the data repository [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]* , required title Full title shown on the page Required, non-empty shortTitle Shorter title for the hub card Optional; defaults to title console Display name of the console; the hub filters by it and it picks the console icon Required, non-empty year Release year, a string Optional contributions {"accepting": true, "guideUrl": "<url>"} shows a Contribute link to that URL; accepting: false hides it Optional; defaults to {"accepting": false} artwork cover is a file name relative to data/<slug>/ in the data repository, width and height its pixel size Optional; add it only after committing the cover ( The site ) The publish action copies this file into game.json on every publish, adding repository (from the CI run's GITHUB_REPOSITORY ), defaultTarget and targets . Changing the presentation is therefore an edit to this file followed by a merge to main ; the next publish of any active target rewrites game.json . config/ci-targets.json { "schemaVersion": 1, "shared": ["src/**", "include/**", "asm/**", "configure.py", "tools/**", ".github/workflows/validate.yml", "config/targets.json", "config/ci-targets.json", "config/site.json"], "targets": { "GAME01-rev0": ["config/GAME01-rev0/**", "orig/GAME01-rev0/**"], "GAME01-rev1": ["config/GAME01-rev1/**", "orig/GAME01-rev1/**"] }, "nonBuild": ["*.md", "docs/**", "references/**", "tests/**", ".github/workflows/review.yml", ".github/pull_request_template.md", ".gitignore", ".gitattributes"] } tools/ci_targets.py reads it in the Plan affected targets job and decides which active targets a push or pull request must build: A changed path that matches Selects a shared pattern every active target a targets.<id> pattern that target, if active a nonBuild pattern only nothing no pattern at all every active target (unknown paths never skip validation) Patterns are fnmatch globs matched against the repository-relative path; * and ** both match across / . Rules: schemaVersion is 1 ; the four keys are exactly schemaVersion , shared , targets and nonBuild ; targets must name every target in targets.json , including planned and archived ones; no pattern may start with / or contain .. . A manual run ( workflow_dispatch ), a push with no known base (first push, force push) and a changed path that cannot be diffed all select every active target. A change that selects no target still runs the Tool tests job and passes the Validate targets check. Adding or changing a target Commit the original to the private repository under orig/<id>/ , add its COPY and checksum lines to the Dockerfile and the image.yml verification, push, and take the new digest ( Build environment ). Add the entry to config/targets.json ( status: active ), its patterns to config/ci-targets.json and its inputs to config/<id>/ . Point validate.yml at the new digest. Push to main . The data directory data/<slug>/<id>/ appears with the first publish. Setting a published target to archived keeps its data directory and history in the data repository, but the site reads latest.json only for active targets, so the page lists it without a measurement. Removing a target from the list entirely removes it from game.json on the next publish; the data directory is deleted by hand, if at all.

title: Build environment
summary: The private image that holds the originals and the toolchain, pinned by digest.
text: Build environment The private image that holds the originals and the toolchain, pinned by digest. CI must build with the original executable, and the original must never be public. The solution is a second, private repository whose only job is to build a container image containing the original and the exact toolchain, and to publish that image to GitHub Container Registry as a private package that the public repository's workflow may pull. The public repository then references the image by digest, so every build runs against a known set of bytes. The private repository Create owner/game-build as a private repository. Copy the three files from the starter kit's build-image/ directory to its root and commit the original under orig/<target id>/ : game-build/ Dockerfile .github/workflows/image.yml README.md orig/GAME01-rev0/main.dol The original is committed to this repository on purpose: the image build copies it in and verifies its SHA-1, so the image can only be produced from the right file. The Dockerfile The starter Dockerfile is a three-stage build for a GameCube or Wii project: dependencies : downloads the binutils and compiler archives, checks their SHA-256 and unpacks them to /binutils and /compilers . dtk : clones decomp-toolkit at the tag configure.py pins, checks the commit and builds it to /dtk . A project patch to the toolkit is applied in this stage. The final image: copies every original to /orig/<target id>/<original path> , checks each SHA-1 against the value you also put in config/targets.json , copies the tools in, and installs gcompat git ninja python3 . Parameters, each marked PARAMETER in the file: the archive URLs and checksums, the toolkit tag and commit, and one COPY plus one sha1sum -c line per active target. The base images are pinned by digest; keep them that way. What the final image must provide, whatever the platform, because validate.yml and the publish action run inside it: Requirement Why /orig/<target id>/<original path> for every active target The Provide and verify target original step copies it into the checkout sh , git , python3 Composite action steps run with sh ; tools/ and publish.py are Python; publish.py runs git log , git clone and git push gcompat on Alpine The Actions runner mounts its own glibc Node.js into the container to run actions/checkout and the token-minting action The toolchain at fixed paths The configure command in validate.yml names them ( /usr/local/bin/dtk , /binutils , /compilers in the starter) The image workflow image.yml runs on every push and pull request: Build image : docker build --tag ghcr.io/owner/game-build:candidate . Verify toolchain inside image : runs sha1sum on each original and probes the tool files. Edit this step to match your Dockerfile ( PARAMETER ). Publish image , on main only: logs in to ghcr.io with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN , pushes the tags :main and :<commit sha> , and appends the image digest ( ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:... ) to the run summary. The job has packages: write ; nothing else in either repository does. Owner setup after the first publish These steps are done once, on GitHub, by the owner: Open the package game-build under the owner's packages and confirm its visibility is private . A package created by a workflow from a private repository starts private; check anyway. In the package settings, under Manage Actions access , add the repository owner/game with the Read role. This is what lets the public repository's workflow pull the image with its own GITHUB_TOKEN . Copy the digest from the Publish image step summary into validate.yml ( container.image ). The public workflow's target job declares permissions: packages: read and pulls with credentials: {username: github.actor, password: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN} . No personal token is involved. Referencing the image by digest validate.yml names the image as ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:<64 hex digits> , never :main . The digest is part of the measurement's provenance: tools/measuring_tools.py extracts exactly that line and the publish action records it as the build-environment tool in latest.json . Changing the digest is a reviewed change to validate.yml , and it is an owner decision: the image defines the compiler and the original, so a different image can change every number. The reference repositories keep the digest line commented with the image workflow run that produced it. Other platforms The pattern does not depend on the platform. For another console, the Dockerfile's dependencies stage fetches that platform's toolchain, the original goes under /orig/<target id>/ at whatever path your build expects (the ORIGINAL constant in tools/verify_target.py and PARAMETER 2 in validate.yml name it), and the configure and build commands in validate.yml change. A single image may hold several targets, and a reference binary from another platform may be added for comparison in the same way; it is just one more COPY with a checksum. Local builds Contributors build locally with their own copy of the game and their own tool installation; the image is for CI. Running the image locally is possible with docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:... sh after docker login ghcr.io , but only for people who already hold the original, because pulling the image requires read access to the private package.

title: Build, verify, measure
summary: Relink the original byte for byte, replace units with source and produce objdiff's report.
text: Build, verify, measure Relink the original byte for byte, replace units with source and produce objdiff's report. Three things happen in one ninja invocation, locally and in CI: the original is split into objects and relinked, the objects marked Matching are replaced by compiled source and the result is checked against the expected hash, and objdiff measures every unit against its original. The publish action reads only the last step's output, build/<target id>/report.json . The commands below are for decomp-toolkit and dtk-template, which the reference repositories use for GameCube. The section at the end says what another platform must provide instead. Local setup for a dtk-template project Start from dtk-template ( configure.py , tools/project.py and the rest of its tools/ ). dtk-template names its config folder after the game ID ( config/GAMEID/ ); rename it to the target id ( config/GAME01-rev0/ ) before adding anything, and use the target id wherever the template says version. Follow its documentation for config/<target id>/config.yml , splits.txt and symbols.txt ; those are the platform-specific part this guide cannot write for you. Wire configure.py to the target list so the active targets are the only versions it accepts and --version takes a target id. Replace dtk-template's hard-coded VERSIONS list with: ```python from tools.targets import registry, build_targets TARGET_REGISTRY = registry() VERSIONS = build_targets(TARGET_REGISTRY) DEFAULT_VERSION = VERSIONS.index(TARGET_REGISTRY['defaultTarget']) ``` and add Path("config/targets.json") and Path("tools/targets.py") to config.reconfig_deps . dtk-template already builds each version into build/<version>/ , which is what makes build/<target id>/ the generated directory. 3. Keep config.dtk_tag and config.objdiff_tag in configure.py as the single place tool versions are pinned; tools/measuring_tools.py reads them, and the Dockerfile builds the same dtk tag. 4. Place your own copy of the original at orig/<target id>/sys/main.dol (the path config.yml and tools/verify_target.py name; orig/*/* is ignored by Git) and verify it: sh python3 tools/verify_target.py --target GAME01-rev0 Configure and build: sh python3 configure.py --version GAME01-rev0 ninja -f build/GAME01-rev0/build.ninja The generated build downloads dtk, objdiff and the compilers at their pinned tags unless --dtk , --objdiff and --compilers point at local copies. The build fails unless the linked executable's SHA-1 equals config/<target id>/build.sha1 , which must equal the original's hash from targets.json . Measure: sh ninja -f build/GAME01-rev0/build.ninja progress build/GAME01-rev0/report.json progress prints the per-category summary; build/<target id>/report.json is the objdiff report CI publishes. This is exactly the command the starter validate.yml runs, after the same configure.py call with the image's tool paths. What the three measures mean Each object in configure.py is declared Matching or NonMatching (dtk-template's Equivalent is for --non-matching builds and never counts). The publish action turns objdiff's report into the contract's three measures: Measure Source in the report What it says linked complete_code and complete_data : units whose metadata.complete is true, which dtk-template's generated objdiff.json sets for Matching objects Bytes that compile from source into the byte-identical executable matched matched_code and matched_data : functions at 100% and data sections at 100%, in any unit Bytes that match exactly, linked or not fuzzy size * fuzzy_match_percent / 100 summed over functions, and over data sections, by the action itself Size-weighted similarity So a NonMatching unit with three exact functions out of ten contributes those three functions' bytes to matched , their fuzzy score to fuzzy , and nothing to linked ; the original bytes stay linked. Promoting the unit to Matching moves its whole size into linked . Function counts come from the report too: exact is functions at 100%, named is functions whose symbol is not fn_<hex> or func_<hex> . File counts treat each unit as a file, named when the unit is not auto_generated and exact when it is named and both its code and data are fully matched. The action checks the report's own totals against its function list and refuses a report whose numbers disagree, so a report from an unexpected objdiff version fails the publish step rather than publishing wrong numbers. Pin config.objdiff_tag and change it deliberately. Partial source Useful partial reconstruction stays in its normal file under src/ and is registered as a NonMatching object. The combined executable still matches because the original bytes for that unit remain linked; objdiff measures the source separately. Reviewers and CI treat matching incompleteness as progress, not as a failure. See Contribution workflow for how partial units are reviewed and promoted. Reading the report The publish action reads these parts of report.json , so any producer must write them the way objdiff does: Path in the report Use measures.total_code , matched_code , complete_code , total_data , matched_data , complete_data , total_functions , matched_functions The summary; 64-bit values are strings, zero values may be absent units[].name Unit name; the unit-prefix input (default main/ ) is stripped for display units[].metadata.complete , units[].metadata.auto_generated Linked status and tool-generated units units[].measures.total_data , matched_data , and matched_code , total_code Per-unit data tile and the exact-file test units[].sections[] : name , size , fuzzy_match_percent , metadata.virtual_address Section extents; sections named in code-sections (default .init,.text ) are code, all others data units[].functions[] : name , size , fuzzy_match_percent , metadata.virtual_address Function tiles and counts Every function must lie inside one of the code sections of its unit, or the action stops with <unit>: <function> lies outside the code sections . A platform whose code lives in differently named sections passes code-sections to the action ( Publishing ). Other platforms The publish action converts objdiff reports and nothing else. objdiff supports several architectures, so a project on another platform that produces report.json with objdiff-cli report generate can use the whole pipeline unchanged apart from these parameters: the original's path under orig/<target id>/ ( ORIGINAL in tools/verify_target.py , PARAMETER 2 in validate.yml , the COPY in the Dockerfile); the configure and build commands ( PARAMETER 3 in validate.yml ), which must fail unless the complete executable matches and must write build/<target id>/report.json ; the code-sections and unit-prefix inputs of the publish action if the defaults do not fit; the TAGS dictionary in tools/measuring_tools.py , which names the version lines of configure.py to report. A project that cannot produce an objdiff report cannot use the publish action as shipped; that is a site-side change and outside this guide.

title: Evidence
summary: Recover what the target supports, record it, and never manufacture a match.
text: Evidence Recover what the target supports, record it, and never manufacture a match. A byte match proves that the compiler produced the same code from the submitted source; it proves nothing about names, types, intent or where the original source file boundaries were. The project's value is the evidence behind those claims, so the evidence is recorded in the repository next to the configuration it supports and is reviewed with it. Inventory before interpretation Inventory what the target and its references actually contain: the parsed filesystem, executables, symbols, debug information, linker maps, diagnostic strings, SDK references and related builds. Record hashes or revisions and which files were parsed. A claim that an artifact does not exist must say how thoroughly it was searched; a file-name search or a few strings is not enough. Related builds (another platform, another revision, another game on the same engine) suggest names and behavior. They do not prove the target's offsets, field widths, original names or source boundaries. Keep target evidence, reference evidence and inferred meaning separate. Bounded tasks Identify the functions, address ranges, candidate source unit, shared headers and dependencies before editing. Confirm accepted declarations on current main . Establish each function's full extent and the limits of any provisional unit; unresolved boundaries stay visible. For a field or signature, cite the actual loads and stores and the relevant caller or callee behavior. A nearby subsystem's access is not proof of the same layout. Preserve unknown offsets instead of inventing a convenient struct. The reconstruction loop Describe the behavior and the evidence-backed types before optimizing for a score. Write plausible source in the codebase's style. Compile with the documented unit or library profile. Compare the full function bytes, referenced data and relocations with objdiff. Investigate the remaining uncertainty, record the result and retain useful partial source. Uncertainty Useful investigation Behavior, references or ownership Target disassembly and bounded static analysis Different instruction selection or scheduling Controlled compiler experiments and the compiler's intermediate output Competing behavioral interpretations A bounded debugger or emulator trace with known inputs and conditions Candidate SDK or library reuse Fingerprints followed by calls, globals, types and boundary checks Record the tested revision, tool version and settings, inputs, conclusion and remaining uncertainty. Check decompiler output against instructions. Runtime observations establish what happened under those conditions, not the original source text. Keep bulk experiments private; retain concise reproducible evidence publicly. The evidence record Each target keeps config/<target id>/evidence.tsv , one claim per row, tab separated: kind start end subject origin start_boundary end_boundary evidence Column Values kind name , function , data , unit-anchor , unit , type , field , external , compiler , assembly , source-form , linker start , end Hexadecimal virtual addresses, end exclusive; - when unknown or inapplicable subject The symbol, source path, type or field concerned origin target (present in the target's bytes, symbols or debug information), signature (a named tool signature), related (another identified build), inferred (interpretation of the code) start_boundary , end_boundary exact , provisional , open or - , claimed independently of each other evidence A reproducible locator and what it establishes and leaves unknown Use separate rows for a name, a function extent, a field layout and a source-unit boundary: one claim never silently proves another. A name row with origin target needs explicit name evidence in the target; a name supported only by behavior is inferred . Compiler profiles are compiler rows at the unit or library level. The starter config/README.md is the full definition and goes into the repository as is. Matching integrity Do not force a match through: per-function flags, optimization pragmas or compiler attributes introduced to force code generation; inline assembly, embedded instruction bytes or patched compiler output in place of compiled source; invented helpers, casts, volatile qualifiers, padding or control flow whose only justification is the bytes; altered symbol boundaries, excluded comparisons or progress categories that hide mismatches; behavioral changes made to satisfy the compiler. Compiler versions and flags need evidence at the compilation-unit or library level. A function-specific exception needs evidence that the original used it and the owner's explicit approval. Originally handwritten assembly needs provenance. Labeling a workaround a fake match does not make it acceptable; it stays a local experiment outside accepted source. When evidence runs out, keep the useful partial reconstruction as a NonMatching unit, keep the original bytes linked and record the gap. Partial similarity is progress; unsupported certainty is not. Imported and SDK code Retain the origin, source revision, license and local modifications of anything imported. A fingerprint match is a candidate, especially for a short function; inspect target-specific calls, data ownership and compilation boundaries before importing. Imported code gets the same accuracy and hostile reviews as new reconstruction. Comments in source explain intent, invariants and non-obvious relationships. Matching scores, compiler experiments, agent notes and review history belong in evidence.tsv or the PR, never in source comments.

title: Contribution workflow
summary: Bounded tasks, isolated branches, independent reviews and an owner-only merge.
text: Contribution workflow Bounded tasks, isolated branches, independent reviews and an owner-only merge. This is the default contribution policy. It is written for people and agents alike: the same rules, the same records, the same gate. The starter CONTRIBUTING.md states it in full and AGENTS.md summarizes it for agents; both go into the repository with the parameters filled in. The owner may adopt a different policy, but then CONTRIBUTING.md , AGENTS.md and the review gate change together. Authority Only the owner ( OWNER_LOGIN ) merges into main . Contributors and agents prepare branches, open PRs and review. A SHIP verdict, a green CI run and an owner clearance comment are three different states, and none of them lets a contributor merge. Optionally, the owner delegates clearance and merging to a merge gate : one agent acting under the owner's account, on a standing basis the owner can revoke. The gate checks reviewer independence, commissions missing reviews from fresh reviewers, posts clearance and squash-merges; it never authors contributions, never pushes to main , and escalates to the owner anything the rules reserve for the owner (matching-integrity exceptions, workflow and approval-control changes, dependency changes). If there is no merge gate, delete that section of the starter CONTRIBUTING.md and the references to it in AGENTS.md . Nobody but the owner changes branch protection, review.yml , REVIEW_OWNER , the build image or its access controls. A dependency problem is reported in an issue, not fixed by changing the dependency. One task, start to finish Reserve. Check open PRs and active branches. Record a bounded reservation in an issue or draft PR: the specific functions or unit, the branch and the shared files it touches. Reserve the batch being worked on, not a subsystem. A reservation expires after 48 hours without a progress update; release scope you abandon, and check existing branches before taking over expired work. Branch. Work on a dedicated branch from current main , in your own checkout or worktree: git switch -c your-task . Branches live in the repository, not in forks; CI refuses to build a fork's pull request because fork builds would otherwise reach the private image. Establish evidence. Boundaries, types and references before source; see Evidence . Search existing headers and accepted units before declaring a shared address. Reconstruct and measure. Compile and compare with objdiff. Keep discarded variants local. Register partial work as a NonMatching object in configure.py so CI measures it; promote to Matching when the unit links byte-identically. The source file does not move on promotion. Record. Add evidence.tsv rows for every name, boundary, type and compiler claim in the same PR. Keep source comments free of scores and process notes. Self-check. Build the complete executable ( ninja -f build/<target id>/build.ninja ) and confirm it still matches; run ninja ... progress and compare with the base revision; list unresolved functions and shared-file changes. Blind accuracy review. A reviewer who did not author or shape the reconstruction interprets the scoped functions with the proposed names and comments withheld, then reconciles that interpretation with the submission and posts an Accuracy: record. Hostile review. A fresh reviewer applies the checklist in CONTRIBUTING.md (source fidelity, compiler settings, types and layouts, names, comments, unit boundaries, comparison integrity, validation) and posts a Hostile: record with SHIP , FIX , REDO or BLOCKED . Resolve and recheck. Fix findings; the reviewer rechecks the delta, not the whole PR, and posts a final-revision record that cites the earlier one. Submit. Fill the PR template: scope, evidence and validation, review records. Request the owner's decision only when CI and both records cover the final revision. Owner clearance and merge. The owner (or merge gate) posts the clearance comment; Owner review clearance turns green; the owner merges. On main , CI builds and publishes. Reviewer independence Independence is about authorship and prior reasoning, not display names. A second agent spawned with the author's conversation is not independent; a reviewer given the task, the target evidence, the relevant configuration and the validation artifacts in a fresh context is. Each record states the reviewer's identity, prior involvement, supplied inputs and the reviewed revision. If isolation is impossible, disclose it; never assert an independent pass that did not occur. Partial source is reviewed for fidelity, evidence and comparison integrity. A measured mismatch is not a finding. A reviewer may return SHIP with documented incompleteness. Rechecks, refreshes and batches After a fix, the reviewer checks the finding, the correction and its affected dependencies and carries the rest of the coverage forward by linking the earlier record and its revision. A replacement reviewer may continue from that record. A full restart needs a concrete reason that invalidates coverage across the PR. After refreshing from main , verify the diff, conflict resolutions and shared declarations, then post final-revision records that cite the earlier ones and name the checked delta. An earlier verdict does not cover a new head; the review gate enforces this mechanically by comparing the revision in each record with the PR head. Compatible bounded contributions may be batched into one PR with each original PR, author revision and review coverage identified; the combined delta is reviewed and CI runs on the combined tree. Compiler-profile and comparison changes get their own review and never ride along in unrelated work. Delivery Every handoff states: changed files, evidence, the validation commands and their results on which revision, unresolved findings and the exact review and publication state. "Implemented", "reviewed", "CI passed", "owner cleared", "merged" and "published" are different states. Do not keep running diaries of agent activity in the repository; PRs and issues are the record. The files File What to fill in CONTRIBUTING.md OWNER_LOGIN , owner/game , the target directory, the README's build section link; delete the merge-gate section if unused AGENTS.md OWNER_LOGIN , the target directory; delete the merge-gate sentence if unused .github/pull_request_template.md Nothing; it is generic README.md Yours: the game, platform, region and revision, the original's SHA-1, the owner, the build commands, links to CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md ; the README is what the other two files point readers at The record formats and the clearance comment the gate checks are specified in the next chapter and repeated in CONTRIBUTING.md .

title: Review gate
summary: Review records, the owner clearance comment and the status check that verifies them.
text: Review gate Review records, the owner clearance comment and the status check that verifies them. The gate is one workflow, .github/workflows/review.yml , that publishes a commit status named Owner review clearance on the PR head. It is success only when the owner has posted a clearance comment that names the current head and links two passing review records on that PR. It runs trusted default-branch code, checks out nothing and holds no build credential; it reads PR comments and writes one status. The starter ships it as review.yml.template together with tests/review_gate.mjs , which exercises the script without GitHub. Review records Each review pass is one PR discussion comment. The first line is the revision, the second the verdict; each header occurs exactly once in the comment, outside quotes and code fences. Revision: FULL_COMMIT_SHA Accuracy: PASS Reviewer: identity and prior involvement Scope: functions, files and configuration checked Evidence: references and validation artifacts used Findings: results, uncertainties and resolutions Revision: FULL_COMMIT_SHA Hostile: SHIP Reviewer: identity and prior involvement Checklist: PASS / FAIL / BLOCKED / justified N/A per category Findings: location, evidence and required correction Coverage: earlier records carried forward and delta checked Accepted values: Accuracy: PASS or Accuracy: N/A - <reason> (the reason is required; a documentation-only change is the usual case), and Hostile: SHIP . FIX , REDO and BLOCKED are valid hostile verdicts but do not clear. The gate parses the headers only; the rest of the comment is for people. Owner clearance After checking reviewer independence, coverage and the resolution of findings, the owner (or the merge gate, acting under the owner's login) posts: <!-- owner-review-clearance --> Revision: FULL_COMMIT_SHA Accuracy: https://github.com/owner/game/pull/NUMBER#issuecomment-ID Hostile: https://github.com/owner/game/pull/NUMBER#issuecomment-ID The marker is the literal first line. The two links point at two different comments on the same PR. To withdraw clearance, edit the latest clearance comment and remove its revision or links; the gate re-evaluates on every comment edit. What the check verifies On pull_request_target (opened, reopened, synchronize, ready for review, converted to draft), on every PR comment created, edited or deleted, and on manual dispatch with a PR number, the job: Fetches the PR. If it is not open, or its head repository differs from the base repository, it stops without setting a status: fork PRs are never cleared. Sets Owner review clearance to pending on the head SHA. Collects the comments by REVIEW_OWNER that start with the marker, takes the most recently updated one, and parses Revision , Accuracy and Hostile from its first three lines. Requires: Revision equals the head SHA; both links are https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/pull/<number>#issuecomment-<id> on this PR; the two links differ. Fetches each linked comment and requires: it belongs to this PR; its first line is Revision: <head SHA> ; its second line is Accuracy: PASS , Accuracy: N/A - <non-empty reason> or Hostile: SHIP for the respective lane. A linked comment that no longer exists makes the clearance invalid. Requires the PR not to be a draft. Sets the status to success with the clearance comment as its link, or leaves it pending . Case Result Current head, owner clearance, two distinct passing records on this PR, PR not a draft success No clearance, or clearance by another login pending New commits after the clearance pending until new records and a new clearance name the new head Same link twice, a link to another PR, malformed headers, a second Revision: line, a failing or stale verdict pending Draft PR pending Clearance edited to remove its revision or links, or a later clearance comment without them pending A linked review comment edited to another revision or deleted pending PR from a fork no status is set tests/review_gate.mjs covers each row; node --test tests/review_gate.mjs runs it and the Tool tests CI job runs it on every push. Installing the gate Copy review.yml.template to .github/workflows/review.yml . The only parameter is REVIEW_OWNER : set the repository variable REVIEW_OWNER to the owner's login (Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, Variables), or replace ${{ vars.REVIEW_OWNER }} with the literal login. The script throws if the value is empty. Copy tests/review_gate.mjs and set its owner and repository constants; run it. Merge the workflow to main first. pull_request_target and issue_comment run the workflow file from the default branch, so the gate does nothing for any PR until it is on main . Open a test PR, post records and a clearance, and watch the status change; post a new commit and watch it go back to pending. Only then, in branch protection for main , require the status checks Owner review clearance and Validate targets , require pull requests, and restrict pushes, force pushes and deletion. Verify who can bypass the rules; a documented policy enforces nothing by itself. GitHub's branch protection documentation describes the options. The workflow's permissions are contents: read , pull-requests: read , issues: read and statuses: write ; it pins actions/github-script by commit SHA. Keep it that way: it is the one workflow that runs on comment events from anyone who can comment. What the gate cannot do It authenticates the owner's clearance and the record references. It cannot prove that a reviewer was independent or that the review was any good; those judgments stay with the owner, directly or through the merge gate. Agents other than the merge gate must not post clearance on the owner's behalf, and clearance never authorizes anyone but the owner to merge.

title: CI
summary: validate.yml: plan the affected targets, run the tool tests, build each target in the image, publish on main.
text: CI validate.yml : plan the affected targets, run the tool tests, build each target in the image, publish on main . One workflow does everything. It runs on every push to main , every pull request and on manual dispatch. Pull requests get the full build and nothing else; pushes to main additionally publish. There is no cache, no artifact and no second workflow to keep in step: the starter validate.yml.template is the whole thing, and the four parameters marked in it are the only edits. Jobs Plan affected targets ──┐ ├──> Validate <target id> (one job per affected active target, in the image) Tool tests ─────────────┘ │ └──> Validate targets (the aggregate check branch protection requires) Plan affected targets Checks out with fetch-depth: 0 (the planner diffs two commits) and runs python3 tools/ci_targets.py . The planner reads the event: for a pull request it diffs the base SHA against the head, for a push it diffs before against the pushed commit, and for workflow_dispatch , a push without a usable before (first push, force push) or --force-all it selects every active target. It applies config/ci-targets.json ( Targets ) and writes two outputs: matrix : {"include":[{"target":"GAME01-rev0"}, ...]} has_targets : true or false Tool tests Runs on the plain runner, outside the image, on every event: node --test tests/review_gate.mjs python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py' -v Add the project's own tests under tests/test_*.py ; they run here. Keep anything that needs the toolchain out of this job. Validate <target id> One job per selected target, fail-fast: false , so one target's failure does not cancel another's build or publish. It runs inside the private image: permissions: contents: read packages: read container: image: ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:<digest> # PARAMETER 1 credentials: username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} env: TARGET_ID: ${{ matrix.target }} Step What it does Require a repository contribution branch test "$SOURCE_REPOSITORY" = "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" , where SOURCE_REPOSITORY is the PR head repository or, outside PRs, the repository itself. A fork's PR fails here, before the original is touched. actions/checkout persist-credentials: false ; the default depth is enough because the publish step only needs HEAD . Provide and verify target original mkdir -p orig/$TARGET_ID/sys , cp /orig/$TARGET_ID/sys/main.dol orig/$TARGET_ID/sys/main.dol , python3 tools/verify_target.py --target "$TARGET_ID" . PARAMETER 2 is the path. Configure target python3 configure.py --version "$TARGET_ID" --dtk /usr/local/bin/dtk --binutils /binutils --compilers /compilers . PARAMETER 3. Build, verify complete executable and measure progress ( id: measure ) ninja -f "build/$TARGET_ID/build.ninja" progress "build/$TARGET_ID/report.json" , then writes the output measured-at as the current UTC time in %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ . PARAMETER 3. The build fails unless the executable's hash matches. List measuring tools ( id: tools ), main only Runs python3 tools/measuring_tools.py and captures its lines in the output lines with a random heredoc delimiter. Publish to the site , main only uses: mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/publish@main with target , report: build/<target>/report.json , tools , measured-at , app-client-id and app-private-key . PARAMETER 4 names the variable and secret. The two main -only steps use the condition github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name != 'pull_request' , so a push and a manual run on main both publish, and nothing else does. Secrets are not available to pull requests from forks anyway, but the fork guard runs first in every case. Validate targets Runs always, after the others, and fails unless plan and tests succeeded and the target jobs either all succeeded (when has_targets was true ) or were skipped (when it was false ). Its name, Validate targets , is the single check to require in branch protection; the per-target job names vary with the matrix and cannot be required one by one. Workflow-level settings permissions: contents: read concurrency: group: validate-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }} A new push to a PR cancels that PR's running validation; pushes to main queue instead, so every main commit is measured and published. The workflow holds no write permission anywhere; the publish action brings its own credential. Installing it Copy validate.yml.template to .github/workflows/validate.yml . Fill PARAMETER 1 with the digest from the image workflow ( Build environment ). Fill PARAMETERS 2 and 3 with the original's path and the configure and build commands that work locally ( Build, verify, measure ). The image's tool paths replace the local ones. Fill PARAMETER 4 with the variable and secret names from Publishing ; the step is harmless until they exist, because it only runs on main . Copy the tools/ and tests/ starter files and config/ci-targets.json . Open a pull request with all of it and watch the four jobs. The first run of Validate <target id> proves the image pull (package access), the original (SHA-1), the toolchain (configure) and the match ( build.sha1 ). Merge. The first main run publishes, provided the credential is in place. What a pull request proves A green Validate targets on a PR means: the tool tests pass, and for every target the change can affect, the complete executable built from the PR's source plus the original bytes for unlinked ranges is byte-identical to the original, and objdiff produced a report. It does not mean the reconstruction is right; that is what the review gate is for. Pull requests publish nothing, so a PR cannot change the site.

title: Publishing
summary: The GitHub App credential, the publish action's inputs and what happens on a push to main.
text: Publishing The GitHub App credential, the publish action's inputs and what happens on a push to main . Publishing is one step at the end of each Validate <target id> job on main . The step is the composite action mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/publish , referenced at @main . It converts the objdiff report into the contract files, validates them, and pushes them to the data repository with a short-lived token minted from a GitHub App. The producer holds the App's client id and private key; the site holds nothing. The credential The credential is a GitHub App installed on the data repository only, with Contents: read and write as its only repository permission (plus the mandatory Metadata: read ). It is not installed on the producer. The action mints a one-hour installation token scoped to the data repository at the start of the step; the token is revoked when the job ends. For the owner's site the App already exists and is installed on mitsevox/decomp-data ; a new game needs its client id and private key as a variable and a secret in the producer repository. For a new data repository, create the App once: GitHub Settings, Developer settings, GitHub Apps, New GitHub App ( documentation ). Any name; no webhook; Where can this GitHub App be installed? Only on this account. Repository permissions: Contents: Read and write . Leave every other permission at no access. Never add Actions or Workflows. After creating it, note the Client ID on the App's page and generate a private key (a .pem file downloads). Install the App on the account, choosing Only select repositories and selecting the data repository alone. Then, in the producer repository (Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions): Kind Name used in this guide Value Variable DATA_APP_CLIENT_ID The App's client id Secret DATA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY The full contents of the .pem file The names are yours; validate.yml passes them to the action as app-client-id: ${{ vars.DATA_APP_CLIENT_ID }} and app-private-key: ${{ secrets.DATA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }} (PARAMETER 4). The reference repository uses the names PORTFOLIO_APP_CLIENT_ID and PORTFOLIO_APP_PRIVATE_KEY . The action's inputs Input Required Default Meaning target yes Target id, as listed in targets.json report yes Path of objdiff's report.json for this target targets no config/targets.json The producer's targets file site no config/site.json The producer's presentation file tools no empty Measured-with tools, one name=version per line; shown on the page as provenance measured-at no now UTC time of the measurement, %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ code-sections no .init,.text Comma-separated code section names; every other section counts as data unit-prefix no main/ Prefix stripped from objdiff unit names for display data-repository no mitsevox/decomp-data owner/name of the data repository app-client-id yes Client id of the GitHub App installed on the data repository app-private-key yes Private key of that GitHub App The starter workflow passes target , report , tools , measured-at , app-client-id and app-private-key and leaves the rest at their defaults. The tools lines come from tools/measuring_tools.py : build-environment=<image digest> , then one line per tag it reads from configure.py ( dtk=v1.8.3 , objdiff=v3.6.1 in the starter). What the action does Splits data-repository into owner and name. Mints the token with actions/create-github-app-token (pinned to its v3.3.0 commit), with owner , repositories: <name> and permission-contents: write . Runs python3 "$GITHUB_ACTION_PATH/publish.py" publish --target ... --report ... --targets ... --site ... --tools ... --measured-at ... --code-sections ... --unit-prefix ... --data-repository ... with the token in the environment variable DATA_TOKEN . publish.py is standard-library Python and runs inside the build image, which is why the image needs python3 and git . publish.py publish then: Reads the report, targets.json and site.json , and builds game.json , latest.json and map.json in memory. repository comes from GITHUB_REPOSITORY ; the measured revision, its commit time and subject come from git log -1 on the checkout; source.url and source.runUrl are built from GITHUB_SERVER_URL , GITHUB_REPOSITORY and GITHUB_RUN_ID . Clones the data repository at depth 1 using the token (sent as an HTTP header through the environment, never on a command line) and configures the committer as <slug> publisher <publisher@users.noreply.github.com> . Up to five times: resets to the newest tip of the default branch, writes the target's files, runs the full tree check, commits as <slug> <target>: <7-char sha>, <n>% code linked with the run URL as the body, and pushes. A lost race (another target or game pushed in between) is retried from the new tip; the write is idempotent, so a retry re-applies the same measurement. Prints published <slug>/<target> <sha> , or <slug>/<target> <sha> already published when nothing changed. Writing the target's files follows two rules that make re-runs and out-of-order runs safe: the first measurement of a revision wins (re-running the workflow for the same commit changes nothing), and latest.json and map.json only move forward by commit time (a slow run of an older commit never replaces a newer one). The history row for the revision is appended either way. The exact file formats are in Data contract . Everything written is checked before the push by the same code as publish.py check , so a bad conversion fails the job instead of landing in the data repository. The target must be active in targets.json ; publishing a planned target stops with Target <id> is not an active target of <slug> . Verifying a publish In the Validate <target id> job log, the Publish to the site step prints published game/GAME01-rev0 <sha> . The data repository has a new commit by game publisher ; its Deploy workflow runs (about a minute). https://mitsevox.github.io/decomp-data/data/game/GAME01-rev0/latest.json shows the new source.revision . https://mitsevox.github.io/games/game/ shows the new numbers. The page fetches the data with cache: no-cache , so a reload is enough. Running the conversion locally The action's script runs anywhere with Python 3 and Git. From the producer checkout, after a local build: git clone https://github.com/mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io site python3 site/.github/actions/publish/publish.py publish --target GAME01-rev0 \ --report build/GAME01-rev0/report.json --repository owner/game \ --tools "$(python3 tools/measuring_tools.py)" --dry-run --output /tmp/tree python3 site/.github/actions/publish/publish.py check /tmp/tree --dry-run writes the files into --output (or a temporary directory) and pushes nothing; check validates a whole tree. --repository is required outside Actions because GITHUB_REPOSITORY is unset; source.runUrl is null locally. This is the fastest way to find out whether a report converts before the first main push, and the only way to inspect the generated files. Before the first push to main The App is installed on the data repository with Contents read and write. The producer has the variable and the secret, and validate.yml names them. config/targets.json and config/site.json validate ( python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py' and a dry run). A pull request has passed Validate targets . Then merge. The first publish creates data/<slug>/ and adds the slug to index.json ; no one edits the data repository for a new game except to add cover art ( The site ).

title: Data contract
summary: The schema-1 files the publish action writes and the checker that enforces them.
text: Data contract The schema-1 files the publish action writes and the checker that enforces them. The authoritative text is contract/README.md in the site repository, and its executable form is publish.py check <tree> : if the two ever disagree, the checker is right. A copy of the contract is in the starter archive. This chapter restates it for the producer's point of view. Layout index.json {"schema": 1, "games": ["game", ...]} data/game/game.json presentation and the target list data/game/cover.webp optional, committed by hand data/game/GAME01-rev0/latest.json the newest measurement data/game/GAME01-rev0/history.json every measurement, append-only data/game/GAME01-rev0/map.json the newest measurement's tile map data/game/GAME01-rev0/contributors.json optional A (game, target) pair is the unit of everything; a game with one target has one entry. Only active targets have a directory. The producer owns config/targets.json and config/site.json ( Targets ); the action derives everything else from them and from the objdiff report. game.json site.json plus repository ( owner/game ), defaultTarget and targets from targets.json , with schema: 1 . Rewritten by every publish of any active target. latest.json {"schema": 1, "game": "game", "target": "GAME01-rev0", "source": {"revision": "<commit sha>", "committedAt": "2026-01-02T00:00:00Z", "title": "<commit subject>", "url": "https://github.com/owner/game/commit/<sha>", "runUrl": "https://github.com/owner/game/actions/runs/<id>"}, "measuredAt": "2026-01-02T00:01:00Z", "tools": [{"name": "build-environment", "version": "ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:..."}, {"name": "dtk", "version": "v1.8.3"}, {"name": "objdiff", "version": "v3.6.1"}], "summary": { "code": {"total": 1618968, "linked": 213044, "matched": 260640, "fuzzy": 292438.68}, "data": {"total": 870056, "linked": 131316, "matched": 157536, "fuzzy": 183267.63}, "functions": {"total": 4746, "exact": 1253, "named": 2595}, "files": {"total": 519, "exact": 119, "named": 374}}, "modules": {"map": "map.json", "contributors": null}} Field Meaning source The measured commit: its SHA, commit time, subject, URL and the CI run that measured it ( runUrl is the provenance) measuredAt The measured-at input, UTC tools The tools input, one object per line summary.code , summary.data Bytes of the original: total , linked (units that link into the byte-identical executable), matched (bytes matching exactly, linked or not), fuzzy (size-weighted similarity; may be null ) summary.functions total , exact (100% match) and named (symbol is not fn_<hex> or func_<hex> ); may be null summary.files Units: total , named (not tool-generated) and exact (named and fully matched); may be null modules map names the map file; contributors names the optional contributors file or is null linked , matched and fuzzy overlap and are never added together. matched <= fuzzy <= total . history.json A JSON array, one row per line, ordered by measuredAt , at most one row per revision: [ {"code":{"total":1610980,"linked":0,"matched":null,"fuzzy":null},"data":{"total":870068,"linked":0,"matched":null,"fuzzy":null},"functions":null,"measuredAt":"2026-10-26T16:34:26Z","revision":"<sha>","legacy":{"provenance":{"kind":"measured","source":"validate.yml run 40360367860"}}}, {"code":{"total":1618968,"linked":213044,"matched":260640,"fuzzy":292438.68},"data":{"total":870056,"linked":131316,"matched":157536,"fuzzy":183267.63},"functions":{"total":4746,"exact":1253,"named":2595},"measuredAt":"2026-10-27T19:52:22Z","revision":"<sha>"} ] Each row carries revision , measuredAt , code , data and functions from the measurement. The action appends one row per newly measured revision and never edits or removes a row. Rows imported from an older system keep whatever they had (missing measures are null ) and their original provenance under legacy ; nothing writes legacy today. The latest revision's row equals latest.json 's total and linked . The site draws the history chart from this file, so the first main publish starts the chart with one point; there is no way, and no need, to backfill. map.json {"schema": 1, "files": [<node>, ...], "sections": [<node>, ...]} : two views of the same bytes. files groups function tiles by source unit (what the page draws) and adds one data tile per unit; sections groups the same functions by code section plus one Data sections group. A node is {"name", "kind": "code"|"data", "size", "linked", "matched", "fuzzy"} plus either address (a leaf) or mapped_extents ( [{"start", "end"}] , hex), and optionally children . Function leaves add "type": "function" , function_address and original_size . The checker enforces that a parent's measures are its children's sums, that extents never overlap, that both views cover exactly the same bytes, that per kind the top-level nodes sum to the summary, and that every function is covered once with counts matching the summary. The action builds the map from the same report as the summary, so a producer never writes it by hand. contributors.json Optional; modules.contributors names it when present. Nothing in this guide produces it: the action writes "contributors": null . The shape, for a producer that adds its own step later, is {"schema": 1, "credited_functions": N, "contributors": [{"id", "login", "functions"}], "functions": [{"id": "<target>:<address>:<size>", "authors": [id]}]} , where every exact function is credited once and the totals agree with the summary. The page shows contributor rankings only when the file exists. Validation rules the producer meets Rule Where it bites Target ids [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ , unique; default listed; platform lower case; sha1 40 lower-case hex; status in active , planned , archived targets.json slug [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]* ; title and console non-empty strings site.json Report function count and exact count equal its measures The objdiff report; a mismatch means a different objdiff version or an edited report Every function inside a code section of its unit; data sections sum to the unit's total_data The report against code-sections Timestamps UTC ISO 8601 measured-at One history row per revision, in measuredAt order Only the action writes it Versioning Adding a field never changes schema ; readers ignore fields they do not know. A breaking change bumps schema , rewrites the whole data repository in one commit and switches the site in the same change; the action at @main follows, and producers pick it up on their next run without editing anything. Writers are strict and readers are lenient: the action refuses anything the checker rejects, and the site shows "unavailable" for a target whose files do not parse.

title: The site
summary: How the data repository is served and read, cover art, URLs and local preview.
text: The site How the data repository is served and read, cover art, URLs and local preview. The site is static. It builds nothing and imports nothing: mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io deploys its own HTML, scripts and this wiki to GitHub Pages, and at view time the page fetches /decomp-data/ from the same origin, which is the data repository's Pages deployment. A producer therefore never needs a pull request against the site. The one thing committed to the data repository by hand is cover art. The data repository's deploy mitsevox/decomp-data holds index.json , .nojekyll , data/ and one workflow, deploy.yml . Every publish is a push to main , and a push made with a GitHub App token starts the workflow, which checks out main and deploys the whole repository to Pages with actions/upload-pages-artifact and actions/deploy-pages . Its concurrency group is pages with cancel-in-progress: false : one deploy runs, one waits, and a burst of publishes collapses into a couple of deploys that each publish the branch tip. Pages serves it at https://mitsevox.github.io/decomp-data/ . For a new data repository of your own: create it public, add index.json with {"schema": 1, "games": []} , an empty .nojekyll and the same deploy.yml , and set the repository's Pages source to GitHub Actions ( documentation ). The site repository's frontend reads /decomp-data/ on its own origin, so a separate site would be a fork of the site repository with that path changed; that is outside this guide. How a page is composed For /games/game/?target=GAME01-rev0 the page reads: index.json , to know the games. data/game/game.json : title, console, year, repository link, contributions , artwork , defaultTarget and the target list. The target picker appears when there is more than one target and groups them by label , then revision . data/game/GAME01-rev0/latest.json for each active target: the summary bars (linked, matched and fuzzy for code and data), the function and file counts when they are not null , the measured commit and run links, and the tools list. data/game/GAME01-rev0/map.json when the summary's modules.map names it: the tile map. data/game/GAME01-rev0/history.json : the progress chart. data/game/GAME01-rev0/contributors.json when modules.contributors names it: rankings. Without ?target= , the page shows defaultTarget . A target that is not active is listed without a measurement. A target whose latest.json fails to load shows "unavailable" and leaves the rest of the game alone; a map or history file that fails the page's checks hides only its own section. The hub at / lists every game in index.json with its default target's code and data bars, the cover, the console icon chosen from console , and the latest commit. Cover art Covers are committed by hand to the data repository, not published by CI, so that rights-sensitive images never pass through the producer or the automation: Prepare cover.webp at the original aspect ratio (the reference covers are 1112 by 1600 pixels). Commit it as data/<slug>/cover.webp in the data repository. The directory exists after the first publish; committing the cover earlier is fine too, since the publish only writes its own files. Add "artwork": {"cover": "cover.webp", "width": 1112, "height": 1600} to the producer's config/site.json and merge. The next publish carries it into game.json . Until both halves are in place the page shows no cover; an artwork entry without the file is a broken image. URLs URL Serves https://mitsevox.github.io/ The hub https://mitsevox.github.io/games/<slug>/ The game at its default target https://mitsevox.github.io/games/<slug>/?target=<id> The game at one target https://mitsevox.github.io/decomp-data/data/<slug>/<id>/latest.json The raw data, same for every file in the data repository https://mitsevox.github.io/wiki/ This guide The site repository's deploy stages one games/<slug>/index.html for every slug in the live index.json , so an established game's page answers with status 200. A game added since the last site deploy renders through the 404.html shell, which is the same application; it becomes a real file at the next site deploy, which the owner can trigger with workflow_dispatch on the site's Site workflow. Previewing locally Clone the site repository and the data repository, then serve the site at / and the data checkout at /decomp-data/ with 404.html as the fallback for unknown paths. The dry-run tree from Publishing can stand in for the data checkout to preview a game before its first real publish. The site repository's README has the same instructions and the test command ( python3 -m unittest discover -s tests ). What never needs a site change Adding a game, adding a target, renaming a title, changing the cover, accepting contributions: all of these are edits to config/site.json , config/targets.json or the data repository. The site changes only when the contract changes or the presentation does.

title: Troubleshooting
summary: Failure messages from the build, the publish action and the page, with their causes.
text: Troubleshooting Failure messages from the build, the publish action and the page, with their causes. Find the layer that failed before changing anything: the plan, the tool tests, the image pull, the original, the build, the report conversion, the push, the deploy or the page. Each layer has its own messages, listed below as they appear in the job log. Plan and tool tests Message Cause and fix Invalid target registry , Unknown target fields , Invalid target identity , Invalid target status , Duplicate target config/targets.json breaks a rule in Targets : exactly the seven fields per target, lower-case platform, 40 lower-case hex digits, status in active , planned , archived . Default target is not active defaultTarget names a planned or archived target. Invalid CI dependency map , CI dependencies must cover every known target , Unsafe CI dependency patterns config/ci-targets.json : the four keys, an entry for every target in targets.json , no leading / or .. in patterns. Diff endpoints must be full commit SHAs The planner ran outside Actions or with an unusual event; run it with --force-all to audit everything. Configure REVIEW_OWNER before adopting clearance The REVIEW_OWNER variable is empty; tests/review_gate.mjs passes its own value, so this appears in the live workflow only. node --test fails after editing review.yml The test reads the script from the workflow file; keep the script: | block and its indentation intact. Image and original Message Cause and fix The job fails while initializing the container (pull denied, unauthorized, manifest unknown) The package is not readable by the public repository, or the digest is wrong. In the private package's settings add owner/game under Manage Actions access with Read, and copy the digest from the image workflow's summary. cp: cannot stat '/orig/<id>/sys/main.dol' The image does not hold that target, or the path differs from PARAMETER 2. Add the COPY and checksum to the Dockerfile and rebuild, or fix the path in both places. Missing/unsafe target original orig/<id>/<ORIGINAL> is absent or a symlink; locally, put your copy there. Original executable SHA-1 differs The file is not the binary targets.json names. Fix the file or, if the file is right, the sha1 field (then the image's checksum line too). Target is not active verify_target.py was run for a planned or archived target. sha1sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match during docker build The original committed to the private repository differs from the Dockerfile's checksum line. Build and measurement Symptom Cause and fix configure.py rejects --version The id is not an active target in config/targets.json , or configure.py was not wired to tools/targets.py ( Build, verify, measure ). The link succeeds but the hash check against config/<id>/build.sha1 fails A Matching object no longer matches, or build.sha1 is wrong. Mark the object NonMatching until it matches; build.sha1 must equal the original's sha1 . ninja: error: ... report.json or no report written The progress / report.json targets need objdiff; check config.objdiff_tag and network access from the image, or pass --objdiff to a local binary. Numbers look wrong on the page but the build is green Compare with ninja ... progress locally at the same commit. linked only counts Matching units; matched counts exact functions anywhere; fuzzy is size-weighted. A new split or a renamed unit changes files counts without changing bytes. measuring_tools: validate.yml names no single pinned build image The image: line is not of the form ghcr.io/<name>@sha256:<64 hex> , or appears more than once. measuring_tools: configure.py has no objdiff_tag The config.<tag> = "<version>" line is missing or formatted differently; edit TAGS in tools/measuring_tools.py or the line. Publish step Every message from publish.py is prefixed publish: and fails the step; nothing is pushed. Message Cause and fix The Mint a data-repository token step fails The App is not installed on the data repository, the client id or private key is wrong or empty, or the App lacks Contents read and write. Check the variable and secret names in validate.yml against the repository settings. DATA_TOKEN is not set The script ran outside the action without the token; use --dry-run locally. --repository or GITHUB_REPOSITORY is required Local run: pass --repository owner/game . Target <id> is not an active target of <slug> The published target is planned or archived in targets.json . targets.json lists no targets , Duplicate target id , Default target is not listed , Invalid target id , <id>: platform must be a lower-case name , <id>: sha1 must be 40 lower-case hex digits , <id>: status must be active, planned or archived config/targets.json ; tools/targets.py would have rejected these too, so the tool tests catch them first. site.json: invalid slug , site.json: title is required , site.json: console is required config/site.json . Report lists N functions, its measures say M , Report has N exact functions, its measures say M The report's own totals disagree with its function list: an objdiff version with different semantics, or an edited report.
